title: Why generics
sub: One piece of code for many types — no object, no casts
cards/0/body: In .NET 1.0, collections stored object. You could put anything in, but getting it out took a cast. Make a mistake and you found out at run time.
cards/0/code:
var list = new ArrayList();
list.Add(42);           // int is boxed into object
list.Add("forty-two");  // a string is fine too
int x = (int)list[1];   // InvalidCastException at run time
cards/1/q: Which line fails at run time?
cards/1/explain: The second element is a string, and the cast to int is only checked at run time.
cards/2/title: List<T>: the type is a parameter
cards/2/body: A generic is code with a type parameter T. The compiler plugs in a concrete type and checks everything up front. Value types are not boxed: List<int> stores real ints.
cards/3/task: Max must compare a and b and work with both int and string. Add the constraint it needs.
cards/4/q: Why can't you call a.CompareTo(b) without a constraint?
cards/4/options/0: Nothing is known about T — an arbitrary type may not have CompareTo
cards/4/options/2: You have to cast to object first
cards/4/explain: A constraint is a promise to the compiler: "T has this."
cards/5/body: For all reference types the JIT emits one shared piece of machine code: a reference is always 8 bytes. Each value type gets its own: List<int> and List<double> each get separate, fast code with no boxing.
cards/6/q: How many machine-code versions of Add do List<string>, List<object> and List<int> get?
cards/6/options/0: Two: one shared by string and object, one for int
cards/6/explain: Reference types share code; value types get their own.
cards/8/q: What do generics give you? Select all.
cards/8/options/3: Code that runs without the JIT
cards/8/explain: The JIT still compiles the code — just for specific types.
